name: Your phone number
plain: A page cannot read the phone number of your phone or SIM.
meaning: No web API returns the device's own number. Proxies: WebOTP reads an SMS code (needs a prompt-free user flow but only the code, only formatted for the origin), Credential Management and Contact Picker give numbers the person chooses.

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

fields.name: proxy: WebOTP API
fields.range: reads a one-time code in an SMS formatted with @domain, not the number

fields.name: proxy: Contact Picker API
fields.range: returns tel values only after a picker the user confirms (Android Chrome 80)

fields.name: proxy: autocomplete=tel
fields.range: fills from saved profile on user action

limits.headline: Can't see your own phone number from a web page
limits.user_action: You type your number, pick one from a contact picker, or tap Autofill
can: Take a one time code from a text message on Android (WebOTP)
Use a number you type in or pick
Fill a number from your saved info if you choose it
cannot: See the number of your phone or SIM
See your texts beyond one matching code
See numbers you did not choose
Get the code unless the text matches the site
limits.reach_label: Only what you type or pick

story.what_it_is: A page cannot read the phone number of your phone or SIM.

marketing.name: WebOTP API
marketing.pitch: Chrome describes filling a one time SMS code for the site after you approve, without giving the number.

story.for_you: A site cannot learn your phone number by itself. You type it in, and later it may fill a code that arrives by text. That is all it gets.
story.for_makers: Phone numbers are very sticky IDs, used to link accounts and track people. The web gives no way to read one. Apps ask you to type it, then confirm it with a code.

use_cases.example: A bank wanted your number for login and sends a code to the number you type.
A chat site wanted to find friends by number and asks you to enter or import it.
A ride site verifies your number with a one time code before booking.
A delivery site texts a code to confirm the number you typed.
A dating site asks you to verify a number by code instead of reading it.
An ad vendor wanted your number to match profiles and gets only hashes you gave.
A fraud team checks that the number you typed matches the code, not the SIM.

legit_uses: None: the browser deliberately withholds it
abuse: Sites attempt proxies to recover it
